methods.notes: The matcher is the same as the Home Assistant integration's manifest: the service UUID or the name prefix, connectable only. The name may be missing from a scan result, so do not depend on it.

identification.notes: Upstream's capture showed an advertisement with no local name. Home Assistant matches the advertised service UUID first and keeps the name prefix as a fallback for scanners that resolve a name. A resolved name is MARPAC_DOHM followed by a per-unit suffix. Upstream also records an aa114b7e-… UUID that early research took for the characteristic. It is not in the GATT table and is not used here as a matcher.

device.name: Yogasleep Dohm Connect White-Noise Machine
device.notes:
The Dohm is a fan-based white-noise machine: a real fan motor, ten speed settings, and no audio files. The Connect model adds BLE so a phone can switch it on and off, set the fan speed (which is the volume), name it, set its clock, and store up to three on-device on/off schedules.
One vendor service carries everything. It has a single characteristic that takes writes with response and sends notifications, and it cannot be read. Commands are short ASCII strings ending in '$', shaped LETTER[,ID[,VALUE...]]$. A lowercase letter is a query and an uppercase letter is a set. Every command except the opening i$ carries the unit's own device ID, which i$ returns. Replies come back as notifications: OK$ for an accepted set, a typed report such as M,1$ or S,03$ for a query, Failed NN$ for an out-of-range value, and an echo of the input for a letter the device does not know.
Replies carry no request ID, so a client sends one command at a time and reads state back after a write. The link needs a BLE bond, and the tested unit kept only one usable controller at a time. A new bond is made after holding the top button for about five seconds.

openness.notes: No vendor publication. One open-source project, which combines a capture of the vendor's Apple-platform app, hardware use through Home Assistant, and a static reading of the Android app. It is the only source, so no fact here has an independent second confirmation.

enter_pairing_mode.notes: No indicator for pairing mode and no window length are documented.

procedures.basis: martinemde/dohm-ble README and pairing guide, from the author's use of their own unit. Not replayed by this project.
procedures.name: Hold the top button for about five seconds

steps.action: Close the phone app, then hold the Dohm's top button for about five seconds.
Pair from the new controller while the unit is in pairing mode.

exclusivity.recovery: Close the vendor app and any other client. If the bond on this controller has gone stale, hold the top button for about five seconds, clear this controller's stored bond, and pair again. Never clear a bond automatically just because the unit is silent: a slow first reply, a wrong device ID or notifications that are not enabled all look the same.

pairing.notes: Upstream reports that BLE pairing and encryption are required on the observed hardware. No PIN or passkey is mentioned anywhere, and the security mode is not recorded, so it is listed as unknown. There is no application-layer login. The Android app asks the OS to bond when it reconnects to a saved unit. Upstream's 0.4.2 release found that forcing an explicit pair on every connection broke working setups, so normal reconnects rely on the existing bond.

unpair.notes: No device-side unpair is known. Pairing a new controller after the button hold appears to replace the old bond on the tested unit. Upstream calls that a hardware observation, not a guarantee.

issued_to_client: device_id: the unit's command address, read once with i$. It is not a secret.
credentials.notes: The device ID is an address that every command carries, not a key. Upstream observed it to be the low three bytes of the unit's BLE address in uppercase hex (00:00:5e:00:53:2a gives 00532A). That relation comes from upstream's hardware, and the Android app does not confirm it. Asking with i$ is the safe route. A host such as macOS that hides the BLE address has to ask anyway.
stored_on_device: BLE bond keys (the tested unit kept one usable controller bond at a time)
Device name, clock, and three schedule slots

factory_reset.description: Upstream documents only the five-second top-button hold, which opens pairing and can replace the stored bond. No source says whether that hold, or anything else, clears the name, the clock or the schedule slots. The README says the onboard clock and settings are lost during a power outage, which may make unplugging the machine the nearest thing to a reset. That claim is untested.
factory_reset.effect: Unknown. No source describes a factory reset.

methods.description: How upstream's standalone client opens a link to a unit it does not know yet. It makes a bond, enables notifications on the command characteristic, sends i$ and caches the ID from the I,<id>$ reply. The vendor app does the same during first setup and then sets the clock.
methods.name: Bond, subscribe, ask for the device ID

steps.action: Close the Marpac Connect app on every phone and stop any other BLE client. The tested unit accepts one controller at a time.
For a new controller only, hold the Dohm's top button for about five seconds to put it into pairing mode. This can replace the bond of the controller that had it before.
Connect and bond (pair) with the unit. Then discover services: numeric ATT handles vary by unit, so resolve 00005601-d102-11e1-9b23-00025b005aa5 by UUID.
Enable notifications on 00005601-d102-11e1-9b23-00025b005aa5 (write 01 00 to its 00002902-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb descriptor).
Write get_device_id (the two bytes i$) with response, and wait for its notification. Allow up to 30 s and up to three tries on the same link for this first reply.
steps.expect: I,<id>$, for example I,00532A$. Store the ID as credential device_id.

steps.action: Optionally send set_clock with local time and ISO weekday. The vendor app does this on first setup and on every reconnect. Onboard schedules depend on it.
Query get_power and get_speed to read the current state.

setup.notes: There is nothing to provision: no Wi-Fi, account or cloud. What a new client must do once is bond (top-button hold) and learn the unit's device ID with i$. After that, every connection is connect, subscribe, then send commands.

rejoin.notes: A new controller pairs after the top-button hold. On the tested unit, this can invalidate the previous controller's bond, so moving back may need another hold. A controller that already has a working bond reconnects without the button.

testing.notes: Not driven against hardware by this project. Every frame is read from martinemde/dohm-ble. Upstream checked power, speed, ID, clock and schedule frames against one PacketLogger capture of the vendor's Apple-platform app, dated 2026-06-02. It also runs power and speed from Home Assistant. The name commands, the slot semantics, the weekday numbering and the zero-padded speed form come from upstream's static reading of the Android app. The t and I commands are inferences that nobody has seen on the wire.

entities.name: Power
entities.notes: State comes from get_power's reply on the same characteristic: M,1$ is on and M,0$ is off (payload_formats.PowerReport). The characteristic cannot be read, so a client polls get_power, and reads it back after each switch since OK$ carries no request ID. Fan speed is not bound as an entity: set_speed takes ASCII decimal text, which no entity role can fill from a number (see protocol_details.schema_gaps).

evidence.documentation_review: One open-source project, read 2026-11-08. Its documents separate captured facts from app-derived facts and from inferences, and this spec keeps that separation through `observed` and `verification`.
evidence.open_questions: Security mode of the bond; whether the five-second hold resets anything beyond pairing; factory reset; S,<id>,0$ behaviour; Failed codes beyond 03; firmware name length limit; t and I support; overlapping and overnight schedule semantics; firmware update path.

initialization.notes: Every reply arrives as a notification on this characteristic, which is not readable, so notifications must be on before the first write (setup.steps; upstream re-arms the CCCD if the first reply never comes).
get_device_id (ASCII i$). The I,<id>$ reply carries the ID that every later command needs; store it as credential device_id. Allow up to 30 s and three tries on the same link for this first reply.

Ack.description: Reply to an accepted set command. Carries no request ID or command letter.
parse_rules: An OK$ cannot be tied to a specific write. After a retry, a timeout or a cancellation, read the state back instead of trusting an OK$.

fields.description: The unit's ID, up to the trailing '$'. Six uppercase hex digits on upstream's units.
fields.name: device_id

parse_rules: Strip the trailing '$', split on ','. Field 0 is I and field 1 is the ID.

Echo.description: Reply to a command letter the device does not recognise: the input comes back unchanged.
parse_rules: A notification that is byte-for-byte the command just written, and is not one of the typed reports, means the device did not understand it.

Failure.description: Reply to a command whose value is out of range.
parse_rules: The notification starts with 'Failed', then a space (not a comma), then a code, then '$'.
The only code seen is 03, for S,<id>,11$. No other codes are documented.

fields.description: The stored name, up to the trailing '$'.
fields.name: name

parse_rules: Strip '$', then take everything after the first ','.

PowerReport.description: Reply to get_power. The report omits the device ID.

fields.description: 1 when the fan is running, 0 when it is off.
fields.name: on

parse_rules: Strip '$', split on ','. Field 1 is '1' (on) or '0' (off). Anything else is malformed.

ScheduleReport.description: Reply to get_schedule: one whole slot in a single report.

fields.description: Stop time, local, HHMM. At or before start means the next day in the app's model.
fields.name: stop

fields.description: Day mask in hex: bit 0 Monday through bit 6 Sunday. 00 means disabled.
fields.name: days

fields.description: Speed, decimal 01-10. 00 means the slot is deleted.
fields.name: speed

parse_rules: Strip '$' and split on ','. Expect six fields. Match the slot number against the slot you asked for, because replies carry no request ID.
Worked: P,1,2030,0730,7F,02$ is slot 1, 20:30 to 07:30 the next morning, every day (0x7f), speed 2.

SpeedReport.description: Reply to get_speed. The report omits the device ID.

fields.description: Fan speed as two zero-padded decimal digits, 01-10.
fields.name: speed

parse_rules: Strip '$', split on ','. Parse field 1 as decimal: '02' is speed 2, '10' is speed 10.

protocol_details.correlation: Replies carry no request ID. A client sends one command, waits for the reply type it expects, and ignores other well-formed reports. For a schedule read, it also checks the slot. Stale reports of the same type and generic OK$ replies cannot be matched to a request after a retry or a cancellation. A timeout does not prove a write failed, so read the state back before retrying a deliberate write.
protocol_details.firmware: The Android app reads the firmware revision string and knows two revisions, 1.3 and 1.6, but none of its commands depend on which one is present. No update mechanism is known.

grammar.encoding: ASCII (UTF-8), no length prefix, no checksum, terminated by '$' (0x24); fields separated by ',' (0x2c); no escaping
grammar.query: Lowercase letter: m power, s speed, n name, p schedule slot, i device ID (no ID field).
grammar.reply: Uppercase short form without the ID (M,1$, S,02$), or OK$, Failed NN$, or an echo of an unknown command.
grammar.set: Uppercase letter with a value: M power, S speed, N name, T clock, P schedule field.

unproven_letters.I: Declared in the Android app as setting the unit number; used only to recognise I,<id>$ replies; outbound form inferred.
unproven_letters.t: Declared in the Android app as getting the time; never sent; reply unknown.

protocol_details.notification_rearm: Upstream saw the unit stop sending notifications on a long-lived link while writes were still acknowledged. Its client rewrites 01 00 to the characteristic's 00002902-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb descriptor before every command, as the vendor's Apple-platform app did in the capture. The Android app writes it once per connection. Where a backend hides the descriptor (CoreBluetooth), the subscription is all a client has.
protocol_details.polling: The characteristic cannot be read, so state means queries. The capture of the Apple-platform app polled m and s about every 5 s, the Android app polls them every second, and Home Assistant polls every 30 s. Upstream also waits about one second after the last command before reading back. That is a starting assumption, not a measured settling time.
schema_gaps: A BLE command parameter cannot name a field of another command's reply as its source; `state:` is network-only. The device ID is therefore modelled as `credential:device_id`, and the step that obtains it (get_device_id, reply I,<id>$) is described in prose. `issues_credentials` needs a JSON reply_path, a cookie or user entry, so it cannot point into an ASCII reply.

A BLE template has no way to say 'this integer goes on the wire as its ASCII decimal text'. Speed and schedule speed are therefore `string` parameters, and no fan or number entity can bind set_speed. Single-digit values (weekday, slot) are modelled as uint8 ASCII codes with labels.

session.notes: These are upstream's values, a known-good envelope rather than protocol constants. On a freshly paired CoreBluetooth link, upstream measured 14.67 s for the first reply and near zero afterwards, whichever command went first. Over BlueZ the unit asks for a slow connection interval, and notifications drain about every 5 s, so 15 s covers two cycles. Upstream drops a link only after three silent 30 s waits, because dropping it early used to cost the bond.

remaining_unknowns: The t (clock query) and I (set device ID) commands are inferred from letter constants in the Android app and have never been seen on the wire. Their syntax, replies and effects are unknown.
The BLE security mode (Just Works or otherwise) and whether notifications in particular need encryption. Upstream reports that a bond is required on its hardware but records no passkey.
Whether the unit really keeps exactly one bond, and whether the top-button hold always replaces it. Upstream calls both observations, not guarantees.
No factory reset is documented. Whether the button hold, or a power cut, clears the name, clock or schedules is unknown.
What S,<id>,0$ does; the meaning of Failed codes other than 03; the firmware's own limit and character set for names.
Whether the device ID is always the low three bytes of the BLE address. Upstream saw it on its hardware, and the Android app neither confirms nor refutes it. Ask with i$ rather than derive it.

Firmware update: none is known. The app reads the firmware revision and knows revisions 1.3 and 1.6, but no update mechanism, DFU mode or image source is documented, so no firmware_update feature is declared.
Schedule edge cases: overlapping slots, start equal to stop, which day an overnight stop belongs to, and whether days 00 and speed 00 really disable and delete a slot on the device.
The aa114b7e-… UUID upstream once took for the characteristic: whether it really appears in the advertisement or was a host-specific identifier.
Battery Service 0000180f-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb is present on a mains-powered machine. What it reports has not been read by any open client.

scheduling.confidence_notes: The wire format is in upstream's capture. The meaning of days 00 (disabled) and speed 00 (deleted), and the default, come from the Android app's model and have not been tested on hardware.
scheduling.device_clock_dependency: Schedules run on the unit's own clock, which only set_clock sets: local HHMM plus ISO weekday, with no date, time zone or DST. The vendor app resends it on every reconnect. Upstream's README says the clock drifts and that the clock and configuration are lost in a power outage. A client that relies on onboard schedules must resync the clock itself, including after DST changes.
limitations: An update is three writes and is not atomic. A failure or a dropped link part-way leaves a mixed slot. Read the slot back after the third write, and roll back yourself if needed.
What the firmware does with overlapping slots, equal start and stop, or which day an overnight stop belongs to is untested.
Times have minute resolution and no date, so there are no one-off events.
scheduling.summary: Three slots. Each holds a start time, a stop time, a weekday mask and a speed. A slot is read whole with get_schedule. It is written with three separate commands, in order: set_schedule_start, set_schedule_stop, set_schedule_days_speed. The app's defaults for a new slot are 22:00-06:00, weekdays (1F), speed 5.

get_clock_experimental.description: t,<id>$, UNPROVEN. The Android app defines a 't' letter labelled as getting the time, but never sends it. This frame follows the query grammar by inference only. Nobody has seen a reply, and its fields are unknown. Upstream expects a T,...$ report, but the device may echo the input, reject it, or stay silent.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

get_device_id.description: i$. Asks for the unit's device ID, the address every other command carries. Reply: I,<id>$ (payload_formats.DeviceIdReport). This is the only command that takes no ID.

get_name.description: n,<id>$. Asks for the name stored on the unit. Reply: N,<name>$ (payload_formats.NameReport).

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

get_power.description: m,<id>$. Asks whether the fan is running. Reply: M,1$ (on) or M,0$ (off) (payload_formats.PowerReport).

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

get_schedule.description: p,<id>,<slot>$. Reads one schedule slot. Reply: P,<slot>,<start>,<stop>,<days>,<speed>$ (payload_formats.ScheduleReport). The vendor app's list screen can send a stray p,<id>,4$. That does not show a fourth slot exists.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id.

slot.description: Schedule slot as one ASCII digit: '1' (0x31) to '3' (0x33).

get_speed.description: s,<id>$. Asks for the fan speed. Reply: S,NN$, two zero-padded decimal digits, 01-10 (payload_formats.SpeedReport).

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

power_off.description: M,<id>,0$. Stops the fan. Reply: OK$. The speed setting is kept, so power_on resumes at the same speed. Read back with get_power.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

power_on.description: M,<id>,1$. Starts the fan. Reply: OK$. Read back with get_power.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

set_clock.description: T,<id>,<HHMM>,<D>$. Sets the unit's clock to local wall-clock time. Reply: OK$. No date, seconds, time zone or DST flag is sent. The vendor app sends this on first setup and on every reconnect. Changing the clock can start or stop an onboard schedule.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

hhmm.description: Local time as exactly four ASCII digits, 24-hour HHMM ('2133' is 21:33). Seconds are dropped.

weekday.description: ISO weekday as one ASCII digit: '1' (0x31) Monday through '7' (0x37) Sunday.

set_device_id_experimental.advanced_reason: Inferred, never observed. If it works, every client that stored the old ID, or derives it from the BLE address as Home Assistant does, stops addressing the unit until it asks i$ again.
set_device_id_experimental.description: I,<id>,<new id>$, UNPROVEN. The Android app defines an 'I' letter labelled as setting the unit number, but uses it only to recognise ID replies. This frame is upstream's inference. Nobody knows whether the firmware accepts it, which values it takes, or whether the change persists. After any attempt, send get_device_id to learn the ID actually in force.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

new_device_id.description: The ID to assign. Format and accepted values unknown; must not contain ',' or '$'.

set_name.description: N,<id>,<name>$. Stores a name on the unit. Reply: OK$. Read back with get_name.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

name.description: The new name. The vendor app accepts letters and digits only, up to 10 characters. That is the app's limit; the firmware's own limit is not known. Must not contain ',' or '$'.

set_schedule_days_speed.description: P,<id>,3,<slot>,<days>,<speed>$. The third write: field selector 3, the day mask and the speed the schedule runs at. Reply: OK$. In the app's model, days 00 disables the slot and speed 00 deletes it. Deleting still sends all three writes.

days.description: Day bitmask as two uppercase hex digits: Monday 01, Tuesday 02, Wednesday 04, Thursday 08, Friday 10, Saturday 20, Sunday 40. Weekdays are 1F and every day is 7F. 00 disables the slot.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id.

slot.description: Schedule slot as one ASCII digit: '1' (0x31) to '3' (0x33).

speed.description: Schedule speed as two zero-padded decimal digits: '01'-'10'. '00' deletes the slot in the app's model; it does not mean silence.

set_schedule_start.description: P,<id>,1,<slot>,<HHMM>$. The first of the three writes that update one slot: field selector 1, the start time. The selector comes before the slot. Reply: OK$. The three writes are not a transaction; see scheduling.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id.

hhmm.description: Start time, local, four ASCII digits HHMM.

slot.description: Schedule slot as one ASCII digit: '1' (0x31) to '3' (0x33).

set_schedule_stop.description: P,<id>,2,<slot>,<HHMM>$. The second write: field selector 2, the stop time. Reply: OK$. A stop at or before the start ends on the next day in the app's model.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id.

hhmm.description: Stop time, local, four ASCII digits HHMM.

slot.description: Schedule slot as one ASCII digit: '1' (0x31) to '3' (0x33).

set_speed.description: S,<id>,<speed>$. Sets the fan speed, which is also the loudness. Reply: OK$. S,<id>,11$ answers Failed 03$. Upstream has not established what S,<id>,0$ does, so to silence the machine send power_off. Read back with get_speed.

device_id.description: The unit's device ID from the I,<id>$ reply to get_device_id (send i$ once after bonding and store what comes back). Upstream's units show six uppercase hex digits, equal to the low three bytes of the BLE address. Never contains ',' or '$'.

speed.description: Fan speed 1-10 as ASCII decimal digits: '1' ... '10'. The bare form ('3') is the one captured working. The Android app sends two zero-padded digits ('03'), and upstream reads that as accepted too.
speed.notes: Written as a string because the wire value is one or two ASCII digits, not a binary byte, so a numeric slider cannot fill it directly. A client converts 1-10 to its decimal text.

characteristics.name: Command and reply
characteristics.notes: Every command is written here with response, and every reply arrives here as a notification. The characteristic cannot be read, so state comes only from queries. The payload is the command's ASCII bytes with no length prefix or checksum, ending in '$' (0x24). Templates below show the bytes. A `string` parameter is spliced in as its ASCII bytes, and the protocol has no escaping, so never send ',' or '$' inside one. Send one command and wait for its reply before the next; see protocol_details.correlation. The longest known command, set_name with a 10-character name, is 20 bytes. That fits the default 23-byte ATT MTU.

services.name: Dohm command service
services.notes: Vendor service on a TI BLE module. Upstream says the UUID family is the one TI's SensorTag uses. The unit also exposes Device Information (0000180a-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb) and Battery (0000180f-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, level 00002a19-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb, read and notify). The Android app reads firmware revision 00002a26-0000-1000-8000-00805f9b34fb before it enables notifications. No open client uses the standard services.
